flashcards.q: What are the four layers of ML monitoring and what does each catch?
flashcards.a: Infra (latency, error rate, saturation) catches the system falling over. Data (schema, nulls, range, cardinality) catches upstream pipeline breakage. Model (prediction distribution, confidence, feature-importance shift) catches model degradation before labels exist. Business (the metric that pays) is the final, slowest-moving arbiter.

flashcards.q: Why is ground truth usually unavailable in production, and what do you monitor instead?
flashcards.a: Labels lag (fraud chargebacks 30-90 days, recs conversion weeks, content-mod maybe never). Monitor proxies instead: shadow/challenger agreement, prediction/confidence drift, cheap proxy labels, sampled human review, LLM-as-judge scoring.

flashcards.q: Why do static alert thresholds page you at 3am for nothing?
flashcards.a: A static threshold doesn't account for seasonality (weekday/weekend traffic mix, Monday ramps), so it either pages routinely on benign variation or is set loose enough to miss a real regression during a quiet period. Fix: seasonality-aware baselines, rate-of-change over absolute value, multi-signal correlation before paging.

An upstream ETL bug truncates a feature (e.g. history window 500→50 events). Prediction mean steps at the deploy timestamp, null rate stays 0% (field is populated, just shorter), infra stays flat, and accuracy stays flat for the full label-lag window (e.g. 2 weeks) because labels haven't arrived. Only layer-3 prediction-distribution monitoring catches it in real time.

flashcards.q: What's the recommended logging/sampling strategy per request?
flashcards.a: Log 100% of cheap structured metadata (ids, latency breakdown, token counts, confidence, model version) always. Sample 1-10% of full-fidelity payloads (raw features/prompt/completion), but always oversample the tail: errors, low-confidence predictions, flagged outputs.

flashcards.q: What LLM-specific signals go beyond classical model monitoring?
flashcards.a: Token cost per request (and per prompt-template version), hallucination proxies (retrieval-groundedness, self-consistency, judge factuality score), refusal rate, and judge-score drift (including drift from the judge model itself being silently updated).

flashcards.q: Give a concrete numeric example of invisible LLM cost drift.
flashcards.a: Average input tokens creeping from 800 to 1,400 (e.g. a prompt template regression) at $3/1M input tokens and 2M requests/month is roughly $1,800/month in pure cost drift, with zero symptom in latency.

flashcards.q: Why does a refusal rate spike sometimes have nothing to do with your own code?
flashcards.a: On a managed/hosted model pointed at a rolling alias rather than a pinned version, the provider can silently update safety tuning, changing refusal behavior with no deploy on your side.

flashcards.q: What makes a monitoring dashboard actually get looked at during an incident?
flashcards.a: It's linked directly from the alert/runbook (not a separate artifact), shows a comparison baseline (now vs last week, not a bare current value), and is small enough (one 'model health' panel per model) for a human to scan in 30 seconds.

flashcards.q: Why should a circuit-breaker-style multi-signal gate exist before paging on model-layer drift?
flashcards.a: Drift alone (e.g. a data or model layer signal) has a high false-positive rate because benign covariate/label shift can trigger it without hurting accuracy. Requiring two layers to agree (e.g. data AND model) before paging reduces false pages while still catching real incidents.

flashcards.q: What's the tradeoff between semaphore-style full-fidelity LLM logging and cost?
flashcards.a: Full-fidelity prompt/completion logging at scale (e.g. 1M req/day) compounds storage cost, observability platform per-event/GB pricing, and judge-scoring compute cost. Design sampling and retention up front rather than retrofitting after a cost or compliance incident.

flashcards.q: When should you NOT build a full four-layer monitoring stack?
flashcards.a: For a low-stakes, low-traffic model (e.g. a weekly-batch model with 200 predictions/day feeding an internal dashboard) — a spreadsheet someone eyeballs monthly is correctly sized; over-instrumenting wastes engineering time better spent elsewhere.

flashcards.q: Rank the two error types a naive alert threshold produces.
flashcards.a: False positives: pages on routine seasonality/traffic ramps until the channel gets muted. False negatives: a threshold loosened to survive that noise then misses a real regression during a normally-quiet period where the absolute threshold was calibrated wrong.

flashcards.q: What is a domain-classifier-style agreement check used as a drift proxy in monitoring?
flashcards.a: Run a cheap fallback model or older model version alongside the current one; track their disagreement rate. Rising disagreement is a robust drift signal that requires no ground-truth labels at all.
